label: Lemma 2.1.
text:
Lemma 2.1.
Let $V$ be a $\mathbb{C}G$ -module with character $\chi$ .
Then the character $\chi_{S}$ of $S^{2}(V)$ is given by
(2.1)
$\displaystyle\chi_{S}(g)=\tfrac{1}{2}(\chi(g)^{2}+\chi(g^{2})),\;\text{for all }g\in G.$
The character $\chi_{A}$ of $A^{2}(V)$ is given by
(2.2)
$\displaystyle\chi_{A}(g)=\tfrac{1}{2}(\chi(g)^{2}-\chi(g^{2})),\;\text{for all }g\in G.$
In particular, for a character $\chi$ ,
the class function $\chi^{(2)}$ defined by
$\chi^{(2)}(g)=\chi(g^{2})\quad\text{for all }g\in G$
is a difference of two characters, namely
(2.3)
$\displaystyle\chi^{(2)}=\chi_{S}-\chi_{A}.$
We denote by $\mbox{\bf 1}_{G}$ the trivial character of $G$ .
Then
$\mbox{$\langle\chi^{(2)},\mbox{\bf 1}_{G}\rangle$}=\frac{1}{|G|}\sum_{g\in G}\chi(g^{2})=:\nu_{2}(\chi)$
is the Frobenius–Schur indicator for $\chi$ .
It is well known that
$\nu_{2}(\chi)\in\{-1,0,1\}$ , and that this value is nonzero if and only if $\chi$ is a real-valued character, and it is 1 exactly if $\chi$ is the character of a real representation of $G$ (see [23, 13.1] or [27, Chap. 4]).
Thus, when $\chi$ is the character of a real representation of $G$ ,
we have
$1=\nu_{2}(\chi)=\mbox{$\langle\chi^{(2)},\mbox{\bf 1}_{G}\rangle$}=\mbox{$\langle\chi_{S}-\chi_{A},\mbox{\bf 1}_{G}\rangle$},$
and $1=\mbox{$\langle\chi,\chi\rangle$}=\mbox{$\langle\chi^{2},\mbox{\bf 1}_{G}\rangle$}$ ,
hence $\mbox{$\langle\chi_{S},\mbox{\bf 1}_{G}\rangle$}=1$ and $\mbox{$\langle\chi_{A},\mbox{\bf 1}_{G}\rangle$}=0$ .
Since all irreducible complex characters of $S_{n}$ are
characters of rational representations, we have
these properties for all $\chi\in{\rm Irr}(S_{n})$ , i.e.,
the trivial character $[n]$ is a constituent of $S^{2}([\lambda])$ ,
but not of $A^{2}([\lambda])$ , for all $\lambda\in P(n)$ .
The main aim of our investigations is to contribute several results
on the characters $S^{2}([\lambda])$ and $A^{2}([\lambda])$ , i.e.,
to provide information on the coefficients
$sg(\lambda,\mu),ag(\lambda,\mu)\in\mathbb{N}_{0}$ defined for $\lambda\in P(n)$ by
$S^{2}([\lambda])=\sum_{\mu\in P(n)}sg(\lambda,\mu)[\mu]\quad\text{and }\quad A^{2}([\lambda])=\sum_{\mu\in P(n)}ag(\lambda,\mu)[\mu].$

label: Lemma 2.3.
text:
Lemma 2.3.
Let $G$ be a finite group and $U$ a subgroup of $G$ .
Let $\chi$ be a character of $G$ , and suppose
the restriction to $U$ decomposes as
$\chi{\downarrow}_{U}=\chi_{1}+\chi_{2}$ ,
with characters $\chi_{1},\chi_{2}$ of $U$ .
Writing $X$ for either $S$ or $A$ , we have
$X^{2}(\chi){\downarrow}_{U}\,=X^{2}(\chi_{1})+X^{2}(\chi_{2})+\chi_{1}\chi_{2}.$

label: Lemma 2.4.
text:
Lemma 2.4.
Let $G,H$ be finite groups.
Let $\chi$ be a character of $G$ ,
and $\psi$ a linear character of $H$ .
Writing $X$ for either $S$ or $A$ , we then have
$X^{2}(\chi\psi)=X^{2}(\chi)\psi^{2}.$
While there is a strong monotonicity property for Kronecker coefficients,
for the symmetric and alternating coefficients less is known.
We state here the semigroup property recently proven by Ressayre [46].

label: Proposition 2.5.
text:
Proposition 2.5.
[46, Proposition 2]
Given $m\in\mathbb{N}$ , we define
$L_{m}=\{(\lambda,\mu)\mid\lambda\in P_{m}(n),\mu\in P_{m^{2}}(n)\text{ and }sg(\lambda,\mu)\neq 0\}.$
Then, as a subset of $\mathbb{Z}^{m+m^{2}}$ ,
$L_{m}$ is a finitely generated semigroup.
In particular, if $\alpha,\beta\vdash n_{1}$ and $\lambda,\mu\vdash n_{2}$
are such that $sg(\alpha,\beta)>0$ and $sg(\lambda,\mu)>0$ then we have have that
$sg(\alpha+\lambda,\beta+\mu)>0.$
3. The class functions $\chi^{(m)}$ and modular decomposition numbers
In this section we want to explain how information on the splitting of squares $[\lambda]^{2}$ gives information on 2-decomposition numbers,
i.e., computing character data leads to information on the
compositions series of the (non-simple) Specht modules $S^{\lambda}_{F}$ for $F$ a field of characteristic 2.
But first we consider a more general situation.
Generalising the class functions $\chi^{(2)}$ defined
in the previous section, one
defines for a character $\chi$ of a finite group $G$ and $m\in\mathbb{N}$ the class function $\chi^{(m)}$ by $\chi^{(m)}(g)=\chi(g^{m})$ , for all $g\in G$ .
This class function is also known to
be a difference of two characters [27].
We start with an easy but useful observation.
Let $C=x^{G}$ be a conjugacy class of the finite group $G$ .
Then we define a class function $\vartheta_{C}$ by
$\vartheta_{C}=\sum_{\psi\in{\rm Irr}(G)}\psi(x^{-1})\psi.$
We note that by column orthogonality, we have
$\vartheta_{C}(g)=\left\{\begin{array}[]{cl}|C_{G}(x)|&\text{if }g\in C=x^{G}\\
0&\text{otherwise.}\end{array}\right.$

label: Theorem 3.7.
text:
Theorem 3.7.
Let $k\in\mathbb{N}$ , $n=k(k+1)/2$ and $\rho_{k}=(k,k-1,\ldots,1)\in P(n)$ the staircase partition.
Let $\lambda\in P(n)$ . Then we have
$sg(\lambda,\rho_{k})-ag(\lambda,\rho_{k})=\mbox{$\langle S^{2}([\lambda]),[\rho_{k}]\rangle$}-\mbox{$\langle A^{2}([\lambda]),[\rho_{k}]\rangle$}=\left\{\begin{array}[]{cl}1&\text{if }\lambda=\rho_{k}\\
0&\text{if }\lambda\neq\rho_{k}\end{array}.\right.$
In particular, $[\rho_{k}]$ is a constituent of $S^{2}([\rho_{k}])$ ,
and for any $\lambda\neq\rho_{k}$ , the Kronecker coefficient
$g(\lambda,\lambda,\rho_{k})=2\,sg(\lambda,\rho_{k})$ is even.

label: Theorem 5.2.
text:
Theorem 5.2.
Let $\lambda\in P(n)$ , $n\geq 4$ . Let
$a_{1}$ , $a_{2}$ , $b_{2}$ and $r_{1}$ be as in Proposition 5.1.
Let
$a_{1,S}=sg(\lambda,(n-1,1))$ ,
$a_{1,A}=ag(\lambda,(n-1,1))$ ,
and similarly define the splitting of the coefficients $a_{2}$ and $b_{2}$
into $a_{2,S}$ , $a_{2,A}$ ,
and $b_{2,S}$ , $b_{2,A}$ , respectively.
Then
$a_{1,S}=a_{1},a_{1,A}=0,\;a_{2,S}=a_{2},a_{2,A}=0,\;b_{2,S}={r_{1}-1\choose 2},b_{2,A}={r_{1}\choose 2},$
i.e., with coefficients as determined above,
$S^{2}([\lambda])=[n]+a_{1}[n-1,1]+a_{2}[n-2,2]+b_{2,S}[n-2,1^{2}]+\text{constituents of depth $>2$}$
and
$A^{2}([\lambda])=b_{2,A}[n-2,1^{2}]+\text{constituents of depth $>2$}.$

label: Theorem 6.1.
text:
Theorem 6.1.
Let $\lambda\in P(n)$ be a symmetric partition; set $d=dl(\lambda)$ .
Then $[1^{n}]$ is a constituent of
$S^{2}([\lambda])$ exactly if
the characters $\{\lambda\}_{\pm}$ are real, i.e., if $n\equiv d\mod 4$ .
Equivalently,
$sg(\lambda,(1^{n}))-ag(\lambda,(1^{n}))=(-1)^{\frac{n-d}{2}}.$

label: Corollary 6.2.
text:
Corollary 6.2.
Let $k\in\mathbb{N}$ , $k>1$ , $n=k(k+1)/2$ . Then the following holds.
(1)
If $k\not\equiv 2\mod 4$ ,
then
$sg(\rho_{k},(1^{n}))=1$ , $ag(\rho_{k},(1^{n}))=0$ .
(2)
If $k\equiv 2\mod 4$ , then
$sg(\rho_{k},(1^{n}))=0$ , $ag(\rho_{k},(1^{n}))=1$ .

label: Theorem 6.3.
text:
Theorem 6.3.
Let $\lambda\in P(n)$ , with $d=dl(\lambda)$ and $r_{1}$ the number of
removable boxes.
(1)
Assume $|\lambda\cap\lambda^{t}|<n-1$ . Then
$sg(\lambda,(2,1^{n-2}))=0=ag(\lambda,(2,1^{n-2})).$
(2)
Assume $|\lambda\cap\lambda^{t}|=n-1$ . Then
$\begin{array}[]{rl}sg(\lambda,(2,1^{n-2}))=1,ag(\lambda,(2,1^{n-2}))=0&\text{if }\frac{n-1-d}{2}\text{ is even,}\\[7.0pt]
sg(\lambda,(2,1^{n-2}))=0,ag(\lambda,(2,1^{n-2}))=1&\text{if }\frac{n-1-d}{2}\text{ is odd.}\end{array}$
(3)
Assume $|\lambda\cap\lambda^{t}|=n$ , i.e., $\lambda=\lambda^{t}$ .
Set $\varepsilon_{\lambda}=(-1)^{(n-d)/2}$ .
Then
$\begin{array}[]{rl}sg(\lambda,(2,1^{n-2}))=\frac{r_{1}-1}{2}=ag(\lambda,(2,1^{n-2}))&\text{if $r_{1}$ is odd}\\[7.0pt]
sg(\lambda,(2,1^{n-2}))=\lfloor\frac{r_{1}-\varepsilon_{\lambda}}{2}\rfloor,ag(\lambda,(2,1^{n-2}))=\lfloor\frac{r_{1}+\varepsilon_{\lambda}}{2}\rfloor&\text{if $r_{1}$ is even.}\end{array}$

label: Theorem 7.8.
text:
Theorem 7.8.
For $k\in\mathbb{N}$ and $n=2k$ , we have
$\-S^{2}([k,k])=\sum_{\lambda\in E_{4}(n)}[\lambda]\;,\quad A^{2}([k,k])=\sum_{\lambda\in O_{4}(n)}[\lambda]\>.$
The above theorem has an immediate consequence in algebraic combinatorics. We recall that $C_{k}=\frac{1}{k+1}{2k\choose k}$ is the $k$ -th Catalan number,
and $f(\alpha)=[\alpha](\id)$ is the number of standard Young tableaux of shape $\alpha$ .

label: Theorem 7.11.
text:
Theorem 7.11.
For $k\in\mathbb{N}_{0}$ and $n=2k+1$ ,
we let $E_{3}O_{1}(n)$ and $E_{1}O_{3}(n)$ denote
the sets of partitions $\lambda\in P_{4}(n)$
into three even and one odd parts, and one even and three odd parts,
respectively. Then we have
$\-S^{2}([k+1,k])=\sum_{\lambda\in E_{3}O_{1}(n)}[\lambda]\>,\quad A^{2}([k+1,k])=\sum_{\lambda\in E_{1}O_{3}(n)}[\lambda]\>.$
There are some further closely related cases that
have nice decompositions.
The decomposition of the Kronecker square $[k+1,k-1]^{2}$
(which is not multiplicity-free)
into its irreducible constituents
can be obtained from the general 2-part formulae,
but is also easily derived from the special formulae for
$[k,k]^{2}$ and $[k,k][k+1,k-1]$ .
For $\lambda\in P_{4}(n)$ ,
we denote by $d(\lambda)$ the number of different parts of $\lambda$ ;
note that here we are also taking 0 into account, so this may be
different from the number $r_{1}$ of removable boxes.

label: Theorem 7.15.
text:
Theorem 7.15.
Let $n\in\mathbb{N}$ and $\lambda,\mu\in P(n)$ such that $\ell(\lambda),\ell(\mu)\leq 2$ .
Then we have
$ag(\lambda,\mu)=0.$

label: Conjecture 10.1.
text:
Conjecture 10.1.
(Saxl’s conjecture.)
For any $k\in\mathbb{N}$ , the Kronecker square $[\rho_{k}]^{2}$ contains all $[\lambda]\in{\rm Irr}(S_{n})$ as constituents.
As mentioned in the introduction,
there is a conjecture (not restricted to triangular numbers)
due to Heide, Saxl, Tiep and Zalesski [22],
which says that
for any $n\neq 2,4,9$ there is some character $\psi\in{\rm Irr}(S_{n})$
such that $\psi^{2}$ contains all $\chi\in{\rm Irr}(S_{n})$ as constituents.
The Saxl conjecture suggests a special candidate for triangular numbers $n$ .
Apart from computational results for (relatively) small $k$ ,
there are already many contributions towards this conjecture that
confirm that several families of constituents occur in the square
(see e.g. [3, 4, 25, 41, 39]).
We have seen above that we may even refine the Saxl conjecture
for certain constituents, as we have found the location (or multiplicities)
of some constituents
in the symmetric or alternating part, respectively.
For example, apart from the constituents at the extreme ends, we had found
in Corollary 3.7 that $[\rho_{k}]$ is
a constituent of the symmetric part of $[\rho_{k}]^{2}$ .
Of course, we cannot expect that $A^{2}([\rho_{k}])$
contains all irreducible $\chi\in{\rm Irr}(S_{n})$
as it does not contain the trivial character.
But computational data suggest that while
both characters $S^{2}([\rho_{k}])$ and $A^{2}([\rho_{k}])$
do not contain all irreducible
characters as constituents,
the number of missing irreducible characters is (perhaps surprisingly)
small.
By Theorem 6.1, $S^{2}([\rho_{k}])$ does not have $[1^{n}]$ as a constituent
when $k\equiv 2\mod 4$ .
Also, we know that $A^{2}([\rho_{k}])$ never contains $[n],[n-1,1]$ and $[n-2,2]$ ,
and it does not contain $[1^{n}]$ when $k\not\equiv 2\mod 4$ .
Based on computational data we suggest the following
strengthening of Saxl’s conjecture:

label: Conjecture 10.2.
text:
Conjecture 10.2.
(Refinement of the Saxl Conjecture)
The symmetric part $S^{2}([\rho_{k}])$ of the square $[\rho_{k}]^{2}$
contains all irreducible characters $[\lambda]$ of $S_{n}$ as constituents,
except for the character $[1^{n}]$ when $k\equiv 2\mod 4$ .
The alternating part $A^{2}([\rho_{k}])$ of the square $[\rho_{k}]^{2}$
contains almost all irreducible characters $[\lambda]$ of $S_{n}$ as constituents,
with the only missing characters being $[n]$ , $[n-1,1]$ and $[n-2,2]$ , and furthermore $[1^{n}]$ when $k\not\equiv 2\mod 4$ ,
and in addition $[2^{3}]$ when $k=3$ .
As stated earlier, Saxl’s conjecture is a refinement in the case of triangular numbers $n$ of a more general conjecture due to Heide, Saxl, Tiep and Zalesski [22], which says that for any $n\neq 2,4,9$ there is some $\lambda\in P(n)$ such that $[\lambda]^{2}$ contains all irreducible characters of $S_{n}$ as constituents.
In fact, the computational data suggest that also this “HSTZ”-conjecture has a strengthening; remember that $[1^{n}]$ is a constituent of $[\lambda]^{2}$ if and
only if $\lambda$ is symmetric, and then we know its position in $S^{2}([\lambda])$ or
$A^{2}([\lambda])$ from Theorem 6.1.
